Recent work supports learning item semantics alongside interaction prediction, but does not directly establish gains for a GRU text encoder trained from scratch. [Recformer (KDD 2023)](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~jmcauley/pdfs/kdd23b.pdf) combines language understanding and recommendation objectives, reporting benefits in low-resource and cold-start settings. [MARS (CIKM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702) learns attribute-aware representations and attribute-wise matching to capture specific preferences that a single coarse text embedding can miss. These motivate task-specific text representations, but their language-model architectures and training settings are not evidence that the same gains transfer to the constrained GRU experiment.

Complementarity should not be equated with textual similarity. [KGSCL (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107191) distinguishes substitution from complementarity when constructing sequence augmentations, but requires explicit Amazon relationship metadata unavailable here. A constraint-compatible hypothesis is therefore one GRU network with randomly initialized token embeddings, separate title/description pooling, and a learned gate combining text with item-ID embeddings; train everything jointly through next-item prediction. Shared tokens may help sparse items, while directional GRU transitions can learn associations between dissimilar items. This is an experimental adaptation, not a published result: histories alone do not establish compatibility or substitute labels. Compare against the corrected GRU baseline using macro validation HR@10; retain one jointly trained checkpoint per category.
